title: The Story of Money · Episode 2
chapters: Bank runs: when everyone wants their money at once
Dollar Bill and the day Australia went decimal

units.t: The Story of Money. Episode two.
In this episode: Bank runs: when everyone wants their money at once, Hyperinflation: when money stops working and Dollar Bill and the day Australia went decimal.
Part one. Bank runs: when everyone wants their money at once.
Your bank does not keep your savings in a vault.
Usually that is fine.
When everyone turns up at once, it can be catastrophic.
Where your money really is.
When you deposit money in a bank, it does not sit in a box with your name on it.
Banks take deposits that customers can withdraw at any moment and use them to fund loans that will not be repaid for years, such as mortgages and business loans.
They keep only a small portion as cash and reserves, betting, sensibly, that not everyone will want their money on the same day.
This arrangement is the heart of banking, turning idle savings into homes and businesses.
But it creates a built-in fragility.
A bank can be perfectly sound, with good loans that will be repaid, and still be unable to hand everyone their money back immediately.
The self-fulfilling panic.
Imagine a rumour spreads that your bank is in trouble.
Even if you think it is false, you have a problem.
If others believe it and withdraw their money, the bank may run out of cash, and those who wait could lose out.
So the rational move is to join the queue.
Everyone reasons the same way, and the fear becomes reality.
Economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig described this trap in a famous 1983 model, showing a bank run can be a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Their work helped earn them a share of the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics, alongside Ben Bernanke, who studied how bank failures deepened the Great Depression.
Melbourne in the 1890s.
Australia knows this story well.
In the 1880s Melbourne boomed on gold wealth and borrowed British money, and land prices soared in a speculative frenzy.
Dozens of building societies and land banks lent freely against property.
When the bubble burst at the end of the decade, borrowers defaulted and many of these institutions collapsed.
In 1893 the crisis reached the major banks.
Depositors rushed to withdraw their money, and many of the colonies' major banks suspended payments within a few weeks.
Some reopened after being reorganised, but savings were frozen or lost, and the colonies plunged into a deep depression that lasted much of the decade.
Melbourne took years to recover.
Stopping the run.
In the film It's a Wonderful Life, 1946, George Bailey calms panicked customers by explaining that their money is not in a safe.
It is in the neighbours' houses, lent out so they could buy homes.
Real banks rely on something more powerful: a central bank willing to lend them cash against good assets in an emergency, acting as a lender of last resort.
The most effective cure has been deposit insurance.
After thousands of American banks failed in the early 1930s, the United States created the FDIC in 1933.
Australia introduced its Financial Claims Scheme in 2008.
As of the mid-2020s it protects deposits up to 250,000 dollars per account holder at each authorised institution.
Because the guarantee exists, the need to use it is far less likely.
Confidence itself is the protection.
Runs in the digital age.
Runs have not disappeared.
In September 2007 queues formed outside Britain's Northern Rock, one of the first visible signs of the global financial crisis and the first run on a British bank in well over a century.
In March 2023 California's Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in a run of startling speed.
Many customers were tech firms with deposits far above the insured limit.
As worries spread through group chats and social media, they tried to pull tens of billions of dollars in a single day using banking apps.
There were no queues outside, just a flood of online transfers.
Regulators closed the bank within roughly two days, showing how quickly modern panic can spread.
The key idea: Banks lend out most deposits and keep only a fraction on hand, which makes even healthy banks fragile.
Part two. Hyperinflation: when money stops working.
Imagine your wages losing half their value before you can spend them.
In Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe, that nightmare became daily life.
Wheelbarrows of cash.
In the autumn of 1923, a German worker might be paid twice a day and hurry out at lunchtime to buy food before prices rose again.
Photographs show children building towers from bundles of banknotes, and people reportedly burned money because it was cheaper than firewood.
By November 1923, one US dollar was worth about 4.
2 trillion German marks.
Lifetime savings were wiped out, and a pension that once supported a comfortable retirement could barely buy a loaf of bread.
This was hyperinflation.
Normal inflation slowly nibbles away at money's value.
Hyperinflation devours it, until people stop trusting money altogether.
What it means.
Inflation is a general rise in prices over time.
Central banks such as the Reserve Bank of Australia aim to keep it low and steady, at around 2 to 3 per cent a year.
Hyperinflation is a different beast.
A common definition, from the economist Phillip Cagan in the 1950s, is prices rising at least 50 per cent in a month.
At that pace prices more than double every couple of months and rise well over a hundredfold in a year.
In the worst cases it is far faster.
Hungary after the Second World War holds the record: in July 1946 prices were doubling roughly every 15 hours.
Episodes like this are rare, but they have happened on almost every continent.
The printing press spiral.
Almost every hyperinflation starts with a government in deep trouble.
It owes more than it can raise through taxes or borrowing, so it has the central bank create money.
In 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied Germany's industrial Ruhr after Germany fell behind on war reparations.
Germany backed passive resistance there, paying striking workers with newly printed money while output collapsed.
When more money chases fewer goods, prices climb, the government needs more money, and it prints faster.
The cycle feeds itself.
Psychology speeds it up.
If people expect money to be worth less tomorrow, they spend wages at once and shops raise prices early.
Economists call this rising velocity of money.
People turn to barter, foreign currency, land or gold.
Once trust is lost, it is very hard to win back.
Zimbabwe's trillions.
One of the best known modern examples was Zimbabwe.
During the 2000s, farm production collapsed after controversial land seizures, exports fell, and heavy government spending was increasingly funded by creating money.
By 2008 inflation was so extreme that official statistics stopped being reliable, with estimates running into the billions of per cent a year.
The central bank issued ever larger notes, culminating in a 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollar note, which soon became a collector's novelty.
In 2009 the country effectively gave up on its own currency, and people began using foreign money such as the US dollar and the South African rand.
Prices stabilised almost immediately once that happened.
Endings and aftermath.
Hyperinflations can end quickly.
Germany's ended in late 1923 with a new currency, the Rentenmark, strict limits on issuing it, and efforts to balance the budget.
Within weeks prices steadied.
The pattern repeats: a new or foreign currency and a government that stops printing to fund itself.
The key is credibility, which is one reason many countries give central banks independence from day to day politics.
The damage lasts.
It hits savers, pensioners and people on fixed incomes hardest, while those with debts, land or foreign currency may come out ahead.
Historians debate how much 1923 contributed to the turmoil that followed, though many say the Great Depression did more.
It did shape Germany's later caution about inflation, and so the European Central Bank.
The key idea: Hyperinflation devours money's value until people stop trusting money at all.
Part three. Dollar Bill and the day Australia went decimal.
On one Monday in 1966, a whole nation swapped pounds, shillings and pence for dollars and cents.
The government's first choice of name, the royal, was so unpopular it was dropped.
Pounds, shillings and pence.
For most of its history Australia counted money the British way.
A pound was worth 20 shillings, and each shilling was worth 12 pence, so a pound held 240 pennies.
Prices were written as £2 7s 6d, and totalling a shopping bill meant constant carrying of twelves and twenties.
Australia had issued its own pound since 1910, but the arithmetic was inherited from medieval England.
By the 1950s businesses, banks and schools were complaining.
Children spent hours converting pence to shillings, and new adding machines and early computers suited tens far better.
Many countries had already gone decimal, and a government committee set up in 1959 recommended Australia follow.
Royal, emu or ming.
Choosing a name proved harder than the maths.
The public sent in thousands of suggestions, from the austral and the kanga to the emu and the ming, a cheeky nod to Prime Minister Robert Menzies' nickname.
In 1963 the government announced the new unit would be called the royal.
The reaction was swift and scornful.
Newspapers mocked it, and many felt it sounded old-fashioned for a young country building its own identity.
Before the changeover the government backed down and settled on the dollar, a name already used in the United States, Canada and elsewhere, and easy to say.
The fuss is a reminder that money is not just maths.
It carries national pride.
C-Day, 14 February 1966.
The changeover was set for Monday 14 February 1966, nicknamed C-Day.
To prepare people, the Decimal Currency Board ran one of the biggest public information campaigns Australia had seen.
Its star was a cartoon character called Dollar Bill, and a catchy jingle sung to the tune of the bush ballad ‘Click Go the Shears’ explained the change on radio and television.
The conversion rule was simple: ten shillings became one dollar, so one pound became two dollars.
Thousands of cash registers and machines had to be converted or replaced.
Old and new money circulated side by side for a while, with shopkeepers giving change in decimal currency to drain the old coins from circulation.
Animals and silver.
Designer Stuart Devlin, a young Australian who later became a famous silversmith in London, put native animals on the coins instead of kings and coats of arms.
The one cent showed a feathertail glider, the two cent a frilled-neck lizard, the five cent an echidna, the ten cent a lyrebird and the twenty cent a platypus.
The fifty cent carried the coat of arms.
The monarch stayed on the other side.
One coin did not last.
The round 1966 fifty cent piece was 80 per cent silver, and as the silver price climbed, the metal became worth more than fifty cents.
People hoarded it.
In 1969 it was replaced by the twelve-sided copper-nickel coin still used today.
Plastic notes, vanishing coins.
The story did not stop in 1966.
In 1988, for the bicentenary of European settlement, the Reserve Bank issued a ten dollar note printed on plastic polymer instead of paper.
It was developed in Australia partly to defeat counterfeiters, since a clear window and other features were very hard to copy.
By 1996 Australia had become the first country with a full series of polymer notes, and the technology has since spread to many countries.
Meanwhile inflation slowly shrank the value of small coins.
In 1992 the one and two cent coins were withdrawn, and cash totals have been rounded to the nearest five cents ever since.
Card payments are still charged to the exact cent.
The key idea: Before 1966 Australians did their sums in a system of twelves and twenties, and a 1959 committee recommended going decimal.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why can a sound bank still be unable to repay all depositors at once?
Answer. Most deposits are lent out for years.
Question two. What distinguishes hyperinflation from normal inflation?
Answer. It destroys trust in money, so trade breaks down.
Question three. Why was the old pounds, shillings and pence system hard to use?
Answer. Twelves and twenties made adding up slow.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
